main.title: Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII
main.summary: Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII is a 2007 action role-playing game developed and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation Portable.

cards.heading: A prequel on PSP
cards.text: Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII is a 2007 action role-playing game developed and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation Portable. The game serves as a prequel to the 1997 title Final Fantasy VII and is part of the metaseries Compilation of Final Fantasy VII, which includes other products related to the original game.

cards.heading: Zack and SOLDIER
cards.text: The game primarily focuses on Zack Fair, a young member of the special forces organization SOLDIER, who is assigned to look for the missing SOLDIER Genesis Rhapsodos. As he searches for Genesis, Zack discovers Genesis' origin, Project G, and its connection to the high-ranking SOLDIERs, Sephiroth and Angeal Hewley. The game's storyline spans the war between the megacorporation Shinra and the people of Wutai to the events in Nibelheim, ending just before the beginning of Final Fantasy VII.

cards.heading: From a proposed port to a new game
cards.text: The game was directed by Hajime Tabata, with Tetsuya Nomura serving as creative producer and character designer. Before development, the Square Enix staff initially planned to make a PlayStation Portable port of the mobile phone game Before Crisis: Final Fantasy VII, but after discussion, they decided to create a new game instead. The plot is based on a scenario Kazushige Nojima had in mind when working on Final Fantasy VII.

cards.heading: Reception and Reunion
cards.text: Crisis Core sold over two million copies worldwide. Critics generally welcomed its story but had mixed responses to the combat system. The remaster Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII Reunion followed in 2022, while the story also appeared in the mobile game Final Fantasy VII: Ever Crisis.

main.title: Halo 3
main.subtitle: The trilogy ends, but the community keeps playing
main.summary: Bungie concludes the trilogy while Forge and Saved Films give Xbox 360 players new ways to change and revisit their matches.

cards.heading: The trilogy reaches Xbox 360
cards.text: Halo 3 reached Xbox 360 on September 25, 2007, with Europe following the next day. Bungie brings its trilogy to a conclusion through a campaign playable cooperatively, alongside competitive multiplayer on Xbox Live. Forge lets players alter maps, and Saved Films allows them to revisit matches from new viewpoints.

cards.heading: Weapons, grenades and melee
cards.text: Weapons, grenades and melee attacks work together. Distance and available cover help determine which option to use, while changes in equipment can make the next encounter play differently. Clear feedback lets players judge when to press forward and when they need time to recover. These familiar actions carry across the campaign and multiplayer.

cards.heading: Sharing a vehicle
cards.text: Vehicles give players shared roles on the battlefield. One person drives while another operates a weapon, making a successful attack depend on both. Larger spaces accommodate these encounters alongside combat on foot. Unexpected movements or collisions can quickly change a plan, producing moments that depend on the players involved.

cards.heading: The cooperative campaign
cards.text: Cooperative campaign play lets a group divide attention between enemies and try different routes. A familiar mission can unfold differently when companions improvise a rescue or recover from a mistake. The objectives remain the same, while the people sharing them change the pace and the memories of each encounter.

cards.heading: Changing maps with Forge
cards.text: Forge allows players to move weapons, objects, vehicles and spawn points within multiplayer maps. Its tools use familiar game objects and physics, making it possible to experiment with layouts and rules inside the game. Groups can turn an established arena into a different kind of match and share their changes.

cards.heading: Watching a match again
cards.text: Saved Films records matches so players can revisit them, change the viewpoint, pause and capture images. It supports studying a mistake as well as sharing an unlikely success. Players use these recordings for montages, machinima and discussions, extending a match beyond its final score.

cards.heading: A connected launch
cards.text: Microsoft presented the September launch as a worldwide event, with midnight openings and releases across dozens of countries. Xbox Live connected those new players to an established Halo community. Online cooperation, multiplayer and shared creations gave the launch an ongoing life beyond the first evening with the disc.

main.title: The Legend of Spyro: The Eternal Night
main.summary: Dragon Time gives Spyro a few slowed seconds to cross a moving obstacle or turn a dangerous encounter around.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: The Legend of Spyro: The Eternal Night is Krome Studios' 2007 action-platform adventure for PlayStation 2 and Wii, continuing A New Beginning. Spyro's visions lead him towards the Chronicler as another threat gathers. Dragon Time becomes the central new ability, alongside elemental melee moves and a longer aerial combat sequence.

cards.heading: Borrow a few seconds
cards.text: Dragon Time slows the action while its meter drains, then needs time to recover. A moving platform becomes easier to cross, and a fast threat gives Spyro a longer opening to act. Krome programmer Chris Lacy described using the same power for timed obstacles and for approaching an enemy when health is low. Those uses put a choice inside a short interval: spend the slowed seconds getting into position, or use them to finish an attack before the advantage runs out.

cards.heading: Put an element into the blow
cards.text: The elements now alter Spyro's physical attacks as well as his breath. Fire's Comet Dash sends him forwards as a burning projectile, while the electric move spins and launches opponents into the air. Airborne combos extend the opening once an enemy has been lifted. Choosing the element therefore changes how Spyro enters a fight and what he can do next. A useful attack creates another opportunity, giving the player a reason to connect movement, element and follow-up rather than repeat a single blow.

cards.heading: Practice before the next encounter
cards.text: Dream sequences provide controlled spaces to relearn Spyro's powers before they are tested in the journey. A rotating platform makes the purpose of slowed time visible, while a group of targets gives a new elemental move something specific to solve. Those lessons sit inside the visions drawing Spyro towards the Chronicler. Returning to the adventure brings the same actions into less predictable encounters, where the player must recognise an opening without waiting for the next instruction.

main.title: Project Gotham Racing 4
main.subtitle: Cars and motorcycles meet changing weather
main.summary: Project Gotham Racing 4 expanded Bizarre Creations' Xbox 360 racing series with motorcycles and weather that could change during an event. Released in North America on 2 October 2007, it kept the relationship between speed and Kudos while giving familiar streets new conditions. Cars and bikes could share a race, so a vehicle's size and movement became part of reading the pack as well as choosing a route through it.

cards.heading: Two wheels join the grid
cards.text: Project Gotham Racing 4 expanded Bizarre Creations' Xbox 360 racing series with motorcycles and weather that could change during an event. Released in North America on 2 October 2007, it kept the relationship between speed and Kudos while giving familiar streets new conditions. Cars and bikes could share a race, so a vehicle's size and movement became part of reading the pack as well as choosing a route through it.

cards.heading: A different kind of balance
cards.text: A motorcycle offers its own ways to earn Kudos, including wheelies and other displays of balance. The rider's body also becomes part of the performance, leaning with the machine and making gestures. Alongside a car, the bike occupies a much narrower strip of road, but the two vehicles negotiate the same barriers and corners. Mixed events turn these differences into an immediate visual contest, with two distinct styles of motion following the same course.

cards.heading: The weather changes the road
cards.text: Rain and snow change the setting while a race is under way. Reflections spread across wet streets, spray trails the vehicles, and visibility can become another concern on the approach to a bend. A route already learned in clear conditions has to be read again through the changing scene. The weather system gives an event its own progression, connecting the appearance of the city with the demands of the next braking point.

cards.heading: A season of competition
cards.text: The revised Career Mode places events within a longer racing schedule. Choosing what to enter and building results gives individual races a place in a continuing season. The original online features included party-based matchmaking and PGR On Demand, alongside tournament and national statistics systems. These extended the series' interest in racing as a shared spectacle: the player's own progress existed beside performances, rivalries and recorded moments from other drivers.

main.title: Team Fortress 2
main.summary: Team Fortress 2 is a 2007 multiplayer first-person shooter game developed and published by Valve Corporation.

cards.heading: The Orange Box and a new Team Fortress
cards.text: Valve released Team Fortress 2 in October 2007 as part of The Orange Box for Windows and Xbox 360, followed by a PlayStation 3 edition. It continued the team-based ideas of the original Quake mod and Team Fortress Classic with nine distinct classes. A standalone PC release followed in 2008, and the game became free-to-play on Steam in 2011.

cards.heading: Nine classes, two teams
cards.text: Players join one of two teams—RED and BLU—and choose one of nine character classes to play as in game modes such as capture the flag and king of the hill. Its development was led by John Cook and Robin Walker, the developers of the original Team Fortress mod. Team Fortress 2 was announced in 1998 under the name Team Fortress 2: Brotherhood of Arms. Initially, it had more realistic, militaristic visuals and gameplay, but this changed over the protracted nine years of development. After Valve released no information for six years, Team Fortress 2 regularly featured in Wired News's annual vaporware list. Finally released on Valve's game engine, Source, in 2007, Team Fortress 2 preserved much of the core class-based gameplay of its predecessors while featuring an overhauled, cartoonish visual style influenced by the works of J. C. Leyendecker, Dean Cornwell, and Norman Rockwell, alongside an increased focus on the visual and verbal characterization of its playable classes and what the developers have described as a 1960s spy film aesthetic.

cards.heading: Characters beyond the match
cards.text: Critics praised the art direction, humour and characterisation of its nine classes. Those personalities also gave fans material for films and other works, some showcased through Valve's Saxxy Awards. The class-based team structure became an important reference for later hero shooters.

cards.heading: Updates and the online community
cards.text: It continues to receive official Valve server support as of 2025, in addition to new content being released on a seasonal basis in the form of submissions made through the Steam Workshop. Since becoming free-to-play, its main source of revenue is microtransactions for in-game cosmetics. A "drop system" was also added and refined, allowing free-to-play users to periodically receive in-game equipment and items. Though it has had an unofficial competitive scene since its release, both support for official competitive play through ranked matchmaking and an overhauled casual experience were added in July 2016. From early 2020 to mid-2024, cheating bots overrunning Valve's official matchmaking servers led to fans holding several online protests, and eventually Valve adding new policies regarding game bans.

main.title: Portal
main.subtitle: Two Openings Change the Way You Think
main.summary: Valve turns two connected portals into a sequence of spatial puzzles, accompanied by the increasingly unsettling instructions of GLaDOS.

cards.heading: Two portals and a way out
cards.text: Valve released Portal on October 10, 2007 for PC and, in North America, Xbox 360 as part of The Orange Box. In Aperture Science's test chambers, the player connects two surfaces with portals and works out how to reach the exit. Momentum continues through the openings, allowing a long fall to become a launch across a room. GLaDOS guides the tests with instructions and promises that gradually reveal another side of the facility.

cards.heading: From Narbacular Drop to Valve
cards.text: The idea grew from Narbacular Drop, a DigiPen student project that caught Valve's attention and led the team to join the studio. Its prototype demonstrated the puzzle possibilities of connecting spaces. At Valve, those experiments developed into Portal's test chambers, story and carefully paced introduction to the rules.

cards.heading: Using momentum
cards.text: Passing through a portal preserves momentum. Placing an entrance below a drop and an exit on another surface can send the player across a gap or towards a high ledge. A room's walls and floor become possible routes once the player understands this relationship. Later puzzles build on the same rule in different arrangements.

cards.heading: Learning through the chambers
cards.text: The chambers introduce buttons, cubes, moving platforms and suitable portal surfaces gradually. A new room often combines something already learned with an unfamiliar arrangement. The player can test an idea and observe its effect before attempting a more complicated solution.

cards.heading: GLaDOS guides the tests
cards.text: GLaDOS delivers instructions while the player works, joining the story to the tests themselves. Her remarks become more suspicious as the purpose of Aperture Science emerges. Erik Wolpaw and the team revised the writing alongside the changing levels, giving the guiding voice a role in the puzzles' tension and comedy.

cards.heading: Revising the rooms through playtests
cards.text: The small team built rough versions of chambers before polishing their appearance. Kim Swift described playtesting from early in development: observing players showed which routes they noticed, where they became confused and how they interpreted a puzzle. The team could then change surfaces, platforms and visual cues before finishing the room.

cards.heading: Launching inside The Orange Box
cards.text: Portal launched inside The Orange Box with Half-Life 2, its episodes and Team Fortress 2. The team's postmortem described the collection as a way to reduce the commercial risk of a short game based on an unfamiliar idea. The bundle introduced Portal to a broad audience while preserving its focused length.

cards.heading: A prototype belongs to a team
cards.text: Kim Swift remembers Narbacular Drop beginning with a practical question: how could the team use portals that David Kircher had been experimenting with? Swift, Jeep Barnett and Garret Rickey had already made student projects together at DigiPen. Their environmental puzzle emerged from several proposals, rather than a complete vision delivered by one designer. In her later account, presenting it at Valve led to an offer to rebuild the idea using Source. The familiar hiring story also contains years of classmates learning to work together.

cards.heading: The unexpected route through a door
cards.text: One Portal room was meant to teach players to carry a box onto a button. Swift recalls that people instead stood on the button themselves, opening a distant door, then fired a portal through it. The team inserted glass so this room would teach the intended action. Elsewhere, they deliberately used the solution those players had discovered. An apparent mistake had produced two useful outcomes: a clearer lesson in one chamber, and an additional possibility to develop in another part of the game.

cards.heading: Ask the player what happened
cards.text: After a playtest, writer Erik Wolpaw asked players to recount the story. When several people missed something, he took that as a reason to reconsider the presentation. Sometimes the team removed information; sometimes it moved a detail into the environment. Swift describes watching expressions as well as actions. A player who solved a room might still be bored or confused about its meaning. Observing both responses gave the writing and level design a shared problem to work on while there was time to change it.

cards.heading: Writing for a voice
cards.text: GLaDOS also developed through repeated recording sessions with Ellen McLain. Wolpaw describes writing towards the actor's strengths as the project continued, rather than treating her contribution as a single final delivery. Her performance helped the team make a machine sound increasingly human as the player's actions undermined it. Swift and Wolpaw's discussion keeps several kinds of authorship in view: puzzles, dialogue, performance and the people testing them. A room could change what the voice needed to say, and the voice could change how that room felt.

main.title: Beautiful Katamari
main.subtitle: Roll up the world after another royal mistake
main.summary: Beautiful Katamari is Now Production's Xbox 360 action-puzzle game, first released in North America on 16 October 2007. A tennis serve from the King of All Cosmos tears open the universe, leaving the Prince to rebuild celestial bodies by gathering objects on Earth. The player rolls a sticky ball that collects anything small enough to attach. As it grows, the same surroundings offer progressively larger targets. The absurd story gives a simple physical activity another cosmic purpose, turning household clutter and city streets into material for repairing a mistake made far above the Prince's station.

cards.heading: Roll up the world after another royal mistake

A tennis serve from the King of All Cosmos tears open the universe, leaving the Prince to rebuild celestial bodies by gathering objects on Earth. The absurd story gives a simple physical activity another cosmic purpose, turning household clutter and city streets into material for repairing a mistake made far above the Prince's station.

cards.heading: Let the growing ball change the route
cards.text: An object that blocks a small katamari may become something to collect after a few more turns. Progress therefore changes how the player reads a familiar area. The best route at one size may no longer be useful once larger objects can be taken, encouraging a continuing reassessment of the surroundings. Rolling with two sticks gives the ball weight and direction, while awkward collections can make its movement less tidy. The pleasure comes from recognising that a space which first seemed enormous has gradually become another layer of things waiting to be gathered.

cards.heading: Katamari visits Xbox 360
cards.text: Jun Moriwaki directed the game, with music credited to Yoshihito Yano and Tetsuya Uchida. A planned PlayStation 3 edition was abandoned, making Beautiful Katamari an unusual Xbox-exclusive chapter in a series previously associated with PlayStation. Japan received it two days after North America, with Europe following in February 2008. Its central activity remains deliberately recognisable. New surroundings and a high-definition presentation give another setting to the change of scale that defines Katamari: the Prince starts by collecting small objects and ends by treating much of the landscape as part of the same ball.

main.title: Every Extend Extra Extreme
main.subtitle: An explosion starts the action instead of ending it
main.summary: Every Extend Extra Extreme is Q Entertainment's Xbox Live Arcade action game, released on 17 October 2007. It develops an idea that began with the freeware Every Extend and continued on PSP: the player deliberately detonates a ship to trigger a chain reaction among surrounding enemies. Success depends on choosing the position and moment that allow the explosion to spread. The screen becomes more crowded as the game continues, increasing the possibilities for a larger chain. Waiting creates opportunity, but it also asks the player to remain safe until that opportunity is worth taking.

It develops an idea that began with the freeware Every Extend and continued on PSP: the player deliberately detonates a ship to trigger a chain reaction among surrounding enemies. Success depends on choosing the position and moment that allow the explosion to spread. The screen becomes more crowded as the game continues, increasing the possibilities for a larger chain. Waiting creates opportunity, but it also asks the player to remain safe until that opportunity is worth taking.

cards.heading: End the chain when the next opportunity is more useful
cards.text: An explosion can pass from one enemy to another, growing the score as the reaction spreads across the screen. The player can halt it to collect power-ups or begin preparing the next attempt. Extra time, shields and changes to enemy speed alter what becomes possible. Losing the ship while unprotected resets the pace and multiplier, making a careless collision costly beyond the immediate mistake. The explosions also add percussion to the music, connecting the timing of a scoring decision to the soundtrack rather than treating sound as a separate accompaniment.

cards.heading: One chain reaction supports several forms of play
cards.text: The Xbox 360 edition includes modes with limited or unlimited time, a more conventional shooting variation and a mode that responds to music stored on the console. High-definition visuals and surround sound extend Q Entertainment's interest in linking simple actions to a larger audiovisual response. Online competition and leaderboards give the score a shared context. The basic action remains unusually economical: the player chooses when to destroy the ship, then watches the consequences travel beyond it. Much of the challenge lies in recognising how much a single well-placed decision can set in motion.

main.title: Ace Combat 6: Fires of Liberation
main.subtitle: A country seen from the cockpit
main.summary: Ace Combat 6: Fires of Liberation is Project Aces' Xbox 360 aerial combat game, first released in North America on 23 October 2007. The player flies as Talisman during a campaign to liberate Emmeria after an invasion by neighbouring Estovakia. Real aircraft inhabit the series' fictional world of Strangereal, combining recognisable machinery with an invented war. Missions move between dogfights and attacks on ground targets, while scenes between sorties follow civilians and military personnel. The campaign gives the fighting a wider setting beyond the pilot's immediate view.

cards.heading: Ask the battlefield to help
cards.text: Allied units do more than accompany the player. Support can be requested during battle, allowing other forces to concentrate on a target or help change a difficult situation. Some missions contain several operations, giving the player a choice about which objectives to tackle. Friendly airfields can provide another practical point within the combat area. The aircraft remains the centre of control, but the battlefield becomes a collection of connected efforts. Reading the map and choosing where to intervene can matter as much as keeping an enemy in the sights.

cards.heading: A new machine for Project Aces
cards.text: The sixth numbered Ace Combat was the first main entry released away from PlayStation hardware. Xbox Live multiplayer and downloadable content also brought new features to the series. Its score draws on composers including Keiki Kobayashi and Tetsukazu Nakanishi, supporting the campaign's large-scale air battles and personal stories. Later Xbox backward compatibility kept the original release available on newer systems. The game is remembered particularly for its allied-support system, which makes the radio traffic around the player part of a battle that can be influenced rather than only heard.

main.title: Castlevania: The Dracula X Chronicles
main.subtitle: Richter's journey receives a new presentation
main.summary: Castlevania: The Dracula X Chronicles is Konami's PSP remake of Rondo of Blood, first released in North America on 23 October 2007. Richter Belmont's adventure uses three-dimensional scenery and characters while retaining side-on platforming and combat. The release also includes unlockable versions of the original Rondo of Blood and Symphony of the Night, bringing the former outside Japan for the first time. Ayami Kojima's character designs give the remake a different visual identity, while revised encounters and obstacles make the journey more than a straightforward replacement of the earlier artwork.

cards.text: Castlevania: The Dracula X Chronicles is Konami's PSP remake of Rondo of Blood, first released in North America on 23 October 2007. Richter Belmont's adventure uses three-dimensional scenery and characters while retaining side-on platforming and combat. The release also includes unlockable versions of the original Rondo of Blood and Symphony of the Night, bringing the former outside Japan for the first time. Ayami Kojima's character designs give the remake a different visual identity, while revised encounters and obstacles make the journey more than a straightforward replacement of the earlier artwork.

cards.heading: Rescuing someone can change the route ahead
cards.text: The remake adds barriers whose removal depends on rescuing particular characters, connecting exploration to the routes that become available later. Other rescue puzzles are altered, and a redesigned fifth stage introduces the Hydra boss. Saving Annette also affects later encounters and the route to the true ending. The player is therefore encouraged to investigate the stages rather than treat reaching the exit as the only useful outcome. A rescued character can change the structure of a subsequent challenge, making an earlier discovery matter again after the immediate section has been completed.

cards.heading: A remake also becomes a route into the originals
cards.text: Koji Igarashi produced the collection, with Akihiro Minakata directing. New voiced scenes can be heard in English or Japanese, while a cooperative Boss Rush uses the PSP's local wireless connection. The unlockable original games let players compare different forms of Castlevania within the same release. The remake preserves the deliberate timing of a side-scrolling action game while reconsidering how its scenes, characters and secrets are presented. Its historical importance also lies in access, finally making Rondo of Blood available internationally alongside the later adventure whose opening returns to the same confrontation.
